source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 50% of people in Canada were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%; satisfaction has deteriorated over the past decade.
29.7% of health spending in Canada was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
9.1% of people in Canada reported unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024 (average of 28 OECD countries: 3.4%).
8% of hospital care costs in Canada were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
17% of outpatient medical care costs in Canada were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
94% of dental care costs in Canada were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
64% of pharmaceutical costs in Canada were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.

While satisfaction levels have decreased on average across OECD countries over the past decade, this masks wide cross-country variation: Türkiye experienced the largest decline in satisfaction of 30 percentage points (percentage points), while Canada, France and New Zealand also had declines of over 20 percentage points Conversely, in Chile and Estonia satisfaction levels increased by 10 percentage points or more.

However, over 8% of the population reported unmet care needs in Latvia (8.4%), Estonia (8.5%), Finland (8.6%), Canada (9.1%) and Greece (12.1%), while in Germany, the Netherlands and Czechia, fewer than 1% of the population reported unmet needs for medical care.
Comparable data for Canada come from the Canadian Income Survey.

On the other hand, this share was less than two-fifths in Canada, Poland and Chile.

In Canada, over one-third of all pharmaceutical spending was financed via voluntary health insurance schemes in 2023, while in Chile and Poland, out-of-pocket payments financed 65% of pharmaceutical spending or more (see section on “Pharmaceutical expenditure” in Chapter 9).

Yet on average across ten surveyed countries, almost one in five people (18%) reported waiting more than a week to see a GP or a nurse, and over half (57%) waited two days or longer, with waiting times longest in Canada, New Zealand and France (Figure 5.13, left panel).
In Canada and the United Kingdom, more than 10% reported having to wait for more than a year (Figure 5.13, right panel).

In Canada, Finland, Sweden, the United Kingdom and the United States, the relatively low number of consultations can be explained in part by the enhanced role that nurses and other health professionals play in primary care – notably in management of patients with chronic diseases and in dealing with patients with minor health issues.
At the other end of the scale, many of the Nordic countries, Canada and the Netherlands had a much lower proportion of spending on inpatient services – at around 20%.
In Austria, Canada, Germany, France, Luxembourg and Switzerland, spending on general outpatient care was much lower overall, accounting for 4% or less of health spending.

With public health emergency measures phased out after the acute phase of the pandemic, the share of preventive spending dropped and reached pre-pandemic levels by 2023, ranging from 6-7% of total health spending in Canada and the United Kingdom to less than 3% in Poland, Belgium, Iceland, France, Switzerland, Portugal and Japan.
On the other hand, Canada, Germany and Mexico spent less than 30% of the total health budget on hospitals.
